title: The Duffel Bag
summary: A luggage-based entrance designed to turn an ordinary airport pickup into an impossible first impression.

steps.text: Choose a destination crowded enough that an unattended duffel bag looks merely inconvenient, not mysterious.
Recruit a friend who can carry the bag, complain convincingly, and never reveal why it is unusually heavy.
Fold the suit carefully, climb inside, and preserve enough dignity to make the eventual entrance look intentional.
Wait until the bag is placed near the intended audience before giving the agreed signal from inside.
Emerge as though arriving by luggage is a perfectly ordinary privilege of international travel.
Introduce yourself before anyone has enough time to ask the practical questions.

title: The Time Traveler
summary: A future-man warning that turns a chance meeting into a supposedly history-altering moment.

steps.text: Approach with the exhausted urgency of someone who has crossed decades for this exact conversation.
Confirm the current year, then react as if the answer has rescued the entire timeline.
Explain that one small decision tonight determines a far more interesting future.
Offer only enough detail to make the prediction sound dangerous to ignore.
Name the rendezvous point where history says the two of you are meant to continue the story.
Leave before the science can be questioned, then return at the appointed time dressed for destiny.

title: The Naked Man
summary: The infamous two-out-of-three gamble: remove every layer and let confidence do the explaining.

steps.text: Wait until you have been invited into a private room and the other person steps away briefly.
Accept that subtlety has already failed and that the next move permits no half measures.
Remove every item of clothing with the speed of a magician clearing a table.
Select a pose that suggests confidence rather than a medical emergency.
Hold the pose when the door opens; explanation only weakens the composition.
Remember the published odds: two successes out of three attempts is still not a guarantee.

title: The Trojan Lesbian
summary: A disguise-and-infiltration play built around becoming the least expected romantic competition in the room.

steps.text: Study the social circle and identify the identity nobody would consider a romantic threat.
Build a disguise around restraint; one exaggerated detail can collapse the entire premise.
Enter as an ally who is interested only in friendship, advice, and an aggressively specific hobby.
Earn trust by listening longer than Barney Stinson normally considers medically advisable.
Allow the disguise to create closeness before revealing that the evening contains a second act.
Exit immediately if the performance becomes offensive, unsafe, or impossible to sustain.

title: The One Week to Live
summary: A ticking-clock story that converts an ordinary night into an allegedly final adventure.

steps.text: Deliver the news quietly: one week remains, and pity is neither requested nor accepted.
Produce a list of final experiences with tonight's companion written suspiciously near the top.
Reject anything expensive, permanent, or likely to require proof of diagnosis.
Choose one joyful plan that can be completed before sunrise.
Treat every interruption as stolen time and every ordinary detail as suddenly profound.
Disappear before day eight requires an explanation.

title: The SNASA
summary: A classified-space-agency identity complete with secret missions, the SMoon, and zero verifiable credentials.

steps.text: Lower your voice and explain that NASA is only the organization civilians are allowed to know about.
Introduce SNASA: Secret NASA, responsible for missions too attractive for public disclosure.
Mention the SMoon once and refuse to clarify whether the S stands for secret.
Treat every basic astronomy question as classified above the listener's clearance.
Offer one impossible detail from orbit, delivered with the calm sadness of a decorated astronaut.
Request immediate relocation before rival agencies compromise the mission.

title: The Cheap Trick
summary: A rock-star impersonation that borrows a famous band's name and hopes nobody checks the bass player.

steps.text: Select a band famous enough to impress but old enough that the current lineup feels negotiable.
Claim to be the bassist; lead singers are photographed too often and drummers invite follow-up questions.
Carry one road story containing a hotel, a broken amplifier, and a city you can locate on a map.
Refer to the band by a private nickname no actual member would use in public.
Blame contract disputes whenever asked to play, sing, or demonstrate rhythm.
Leave for the fictional tour bus before somebody opens a search engine.

title: My Penis Grants Wishes
summary: A genie costume, a magical claim, and perhaps the lowest clearance requirement in the entire archive.

steps.text: Acquire a genie costume that reads mystical rather than children's birthday entertainer.
Announce that the lamp has been misplaced but its wish-granting power found a new residence.
Limit the offer to three wishes; even fictional magic requires disciplined boundaries.
Reject wishes involving money, immortality, or verifiable outcomes.
Present the activation ritual with absolute confidence and no supporting evidence.
If the room does not laugh, bow, vanish, and reconsider the entire branch of magical jurisprudence.

title: He's Not Coming
summary: A romantic-observation-deck ambush powered by one ominous sentence and relentless repetition.

steps.text: Go to the observation deck where grand romantic gestures are statistically overrepresented.
Find someone waiting alone and approach with the solemnity of a messenger in a rainstorm.
Say only, ‘He's not coming,’ then let the skyline perform the dramatic underscore.
If corrected, apologize and repeat the line to the next person waiting.
Continue until coincidence turns the sentence into devastatingly accurate news.
Offer a shoulder, a warm drink, and no explanation for how you supposedly knew.

title: Don't Drink That
summary: A fake rescue in which a perfectly safe drink becomes evidence of another man's villainy.

steps.text: Spot the glass just before it reaches its owner and interrupt with credible urgency.
Warn the owner not to drink it, without saying anything specific enough to be disproved.
Glance toward the designated fall guy as though deciding whether to expose him.
Explain that you saw something suspicious and could not remain silent.
Accept gratitude with the burdened expression of a reluctant hero.
End the play before the bartender, the fall guy, or basic chemistry enters the conversation.

title: The Ted Mosby
summary: A borrowed identity, an abandoned-at-the-altar story, and a red cowboy boot level of emotional specificity.

steps.text: Dress like Ted Mosby: earnest layers, architectural opinions, and one accessory nobody requested.
Introduce yourself as Ted and establish that romance has recently dealt a spectacular public defeat.
Describe the altar, the note, and the rain with exactly one detail too poetic to challenge.
Insist you are not looking for sympathy while arranging every sentence to receive it.
Let the listener restore your faith in serendipity over one drink.
Leave before the actual Ted Mosby arrives to object on both moral and sartorial grounds.

title: Mrs. Stinsfire
summary: An elaborate housekeeper disguise whose commitment vastly exceeds the wisdom of its objective.

steps.text: Build an older housekeeper persona with a name, accent, backstory, and deeply held opinions about dust.
Use professional makeup and wardrobe; a half disguise creates twice the suspicion.
Secure legitimate access to the location rather than appearing mysteriously beside a laundry cart.
Remain helpful enough that nobody questions why the new housekeeper asks so many personal questions.
Never break character, especially when carrying something heavy or hearing your real name.
Retire Mrs. Stinsfire the moment the disguise violates privacy, consent, or common sense.

title: Lorenzo Von Matterhorn
summary: A search-engine illusion that turns a fabricated nobleman into the most documented stranger in the bar.

steps.text: Invent a name so aristocratic it sounds expensive when whispered: Lorenzo Von Matterhorn.
Create a network of polished websites describing wealth, bravery, philanthropy, and one tasteful tragedy.
Ensure the pages agree on dates, titles, and the small European jurisdiction that supposedly granted them.
Meet the target without volunteering the name; manufactured curiosity must do the searching.
React to recognition with weary humility, as though fame is the least interesting burden you carry.
Disappear before reverse-image search, journalism, or an actual European enters the room.

title: The Scuba Diver
summary: The Playbook episode's nested master play, engineered to prove that Barney could execute the impossible final page.

steps.text: Announce retirement from the Playbook loudly enough that disbelief becomes the first ingredient.
Arrange for the final page to appear more outrageous than every play that came before it.
Let the gang challenge the premise and believe the challenge belongs to them.
Build a chain of apparent failures that quietly moves every participant into position.
Wear the scuba suit even when no body of water is available; commitment is the camouflage.
Reveal that the failed plays, the witnesses, and the final target were one continuous design.
Accept victory only after the mark recognizes that the story itself was the real Scuba Diver.

title: The Call Barney Stinson
summary: A Super Bowl-scale advertisement whose only product is the telephone number of Barney Stinson.

steps.text: Acquire the most visible advertising placement available during the most watched event possible.
Remove every distraction: no company, no slogan, no product, only a name and a number.
Pose beside the number with the confidence of a man already expecting national curiosity.
Keep every phone charged and every line staffed by the same person: Barney Stinson.
Answer each call as though it is the one the entire campaign was designed to receive.
Retire the number before curiosity becomes litigation.

title: The Two Can Play at That Game
summary: A counter-play activated when the other player believes they are already controlling the board.

steps.text: Recognize the moment someone begins a play and resist the urge to expose it immediately.
Allow the first move to succeed just enough that its author becomes confident.
Mirror the premise with one detail changed, forcing the original player to react instead of plan.
Feed each reaction back into the counter-play while maintaining plausible innocence.
Reveal nothing until both versions of the game occupy the same room.
End with the only winning line available: two can play at that game.

title: The Robin
summary: Barney's final and most personal play: an elaborate path from denial to a rooftop proposal.

steps.text: Admit to yourself you still have feelings for this girl: “I am hopelessly, irretrievably in love with her. More than she knows.”
Choose the completely wrong moment to make a drunken move after hanging out at a strip club. And get shot down on purpose.
Agree that you two don't work, locking the door on any future you could have together. “I'm done trying to get you. I can't do it anymore,” which will drive Robin nuts.
Robin goes nuts.
Find the person who annoys Robin most in the world and ask for her help. Explain everything to Patrice and hope she agrees to help.
Check with your doctor about possible broken ribs.
Pretend to be dating Patrice.
Wait until Robin inevitably breaks into your place to find The Playbook and show it to Patrice, which you'll monitor via the hidden cameras you have in your apartment.
After Patrice finds The Playbook, have your first big fight.
Prove your loyalty to Patrice by burning The Playbook. And actually burn it. You don't need it anymore.
Because your friends have no boundaries, they'll inevitably have an intervention for Robin, which you'll monitor via the hidden cameras you have in Marshall and Lily's apartment.
Tell only Ted about your plan to propose to Patrice.
Wait and see if Ted tells Robin, and if he does, it means your best bro in the world has let go of Robin and has given you his blessing.
Robin arrives at her favorite spot in the city and finds the secret final page of The Playbook, the last play you'll ever run.
Robin realizes she's standing underneath a mistletoe.

title: The Royal Archduke of Grand Fenwick
summary: A portrait-backed aristocratic identity from a nation too small for anyone to confidently disprove.

steps.text: Select a country obscure enough to sound plausible and grand enough to imply ceremonial authority.
Commission a portrait containing a sash, a severe chair, and at least one inherited expression.
Introduce yourself with the full title only once; repetition makes nobility look needy.
Describe state duties using words like diplomatic, succession, and regatta.
Treat local customs as charmingly unfamiliar, especially the custom of paying for drinks.
Depart when anyone asks to locate Grand Fenwick on a map.

title: The Weekend at Barney's
summary: A Weekend at Bernie's-inspired concept whose title promises disguise, confusion, and terrible judgment.

steps.text: Choose a weekend where every sensible plan has already failed.
Construct a scenario requiring one apparently unavailable participant to remain socially present.
Use sunglasses, strategic seating, and friends with more loyalty than judgment.
Keep the group moving; stillness invites questions and questions invite consequences.
Turn every near discovery into evidence that the performance is working.
Abandon the play before an homage becomes an incident report.

title: The Special Delivery
summary: A courier disguise that makes the introduction arrive before the suspicion.

steps.text: Prepare a package impressive enough to open a door but harmless enough to survive inspection.
Dress as the kind of courier nobody remembers five minutes after signing.
Confirm the recipient's name and announce a delivery requiring personal attention.
Reveal a charming surprise instead of the ordinary contents the box appears to promise.
Use the delivery window to make one concise invitation, not a full sales presentation.
Leave the package behind only if it is genuinely welcome.

title: The Kidney
summary: A medical-emergency melodrama that mistakes organ-level urgency for an opening line.

steps.text: Mention that a kidney has become central to the evening, then pause before explaining whose.
Carry a hospital bracelet, a donor card, and a story medically vague enough to survive one question.
Describe the search for a compatible stranger as both tragic and improbably romantic.
Reject any offer involving an actual procedure, ambulance, or licensed professional.
Convert the supposed last healthy evening into one modest drink together.
Retire the diagnosis permanently before karma requests documentation.

title: The I Have a Pet Loch Ness Monster
summary: A cryptozoological boast supported by blurry evidence and an even blurrier Scottish property claim.

steps.text: Casually mention the family estate on Loch Ness as though every family has one.
Refer to the monster by a private nickname and correct anyone who calls it Nessie.
Produce one dark photograph containing water, fog, and a shape no expert could responsibly identify.
Explain that secrecy protects the creature from scientists and protects you from follow-up questions.
Offer a future visit to the estate after sufficient trust has been established.
Change subjects before anyone checks flight prices to Scotland.

title: The Mannequin
summary: A Playbook II concept built around perfect stillness, retail camouflage, and a precisely timed reveal.

steps.text: Choose a display window with flattering light, limited security, and mannequins wearing approximately your size.
Match the pose, expression, and profound emotional vacancy of the surrounding display.
Remain motionless while the intended audience approaches; blinking is an amateur confession.
Move only after eye contact makes the impossible reveal unavoidable.
Deliver the invitation as though fate, not retail trespass, placed you behind the glass.
Exit before store management updates the display.

title: The Jim Nacho
summary: A celebrity-chef identity in which confidence supplies the fame and nachos supply the supporting evidence.

steps.text: Invent a chef named Jim Nacho and behave as though the name already headlines restaurants worldwide.
Carry one signature seasoning in an unlabelled silver tin.
Describe nachos with the vocabulary normally reserved for architecture and fine wine.
Order for the table, then make one tiny adjustment the kitchen cannot possibly verify.
Accept recognition humbly even when nobody has actually recognized you.
Leave behind the recipe only if it contains no measurements and at least one secret ingredient.

title: The Rumspringa
summary: A traveler-on-one-night-of-freedom story with plain clothes, enormous curiosity, and a strict sunrise deadline.

steps.text: Arrive dressed with deliberate simplicity and regard every modern object with disciplined wonder.
Explain that tonight is a rare excursion beyond an extremely sheltered community.
Ask for guidance through three ordinary experiences as though each is forbidden knowledge.
Choose pleasures that are safe, public, and unlikely to require a permanent record.
Treat the companion as the trusted guide to an entirely new world.
Return before sunrise, leaving the future of the story to mystery rather than impersonation.

title: The I Only Have One Day Left to Live
summary: The accelerated successor to One Week to Live, reducing the countdown to a single allegedly final night.

steps.text: Reveal that only one day remains and refuse to waste any of it explaining the diagnosis.
Present a final-day list short enough to finish and dramatic enough to invite company.
Choose one meal, one view, one dance, and one honest-sounding confession.
Keep every plan within walking distance; a ticking clock should not depend on traffic.
End the night with gratitude instead of promises about tomorrow.
Do not repeat the play anywhere the supposedly final survivor might be recognized.
